441.event_title: Liu Bei wins Zhuge Liang as his adviser
441.event: Liu Bei, at the time a minor warlord without a secure base, sought out the scholar Zhuge Liang, who was living in retirement at Longzhong, and persuaded him to enter his service as an adviser. Zhuge Liang helped him organise a large army, urged an alliance with Sun Quan that led to victory over Cao Cao at the Red Cliffs in 208, and helped him found the Shu-Han state in 221. On his deathbed Liu Bei urged his son to rely on Zhuge Liang's advice.
441.explanation: Liu Bei's rise from a wandering commander to an emperor rested heavily on the wise counsellor he had deliberately sought and kept.
441.tie_back: The kural advises learning the right way to win, and then securing, the friendship of the wise and mature, and Liu Bei's pursuit of Zhuge Liang became the classic Chinese example of doing so.
441._accuracy_note: A strong fit for seeking out and securing a wise adviser; the popular tale of three visits to his cottage is treated by Britannica as legend and is left out here.

442.event_title: Koprulu Mehmed Pasha becomes Ottoman grand vizier
442.event: In 1656, after the Venetians defeated the Ottoman fleet at the Dardanelles and occupied nearby islands, the court of the young sultan Mehmed IV appointed the elderly provincial governor Koprulu Mehmed Pasha as grand vizier, on his condition that he be allowed to govern without interference. He suppressed rebellious governors and rivals, reorganised the army and rebuilt the fleet, which recovered islands lost to Venice in 1657. Members of his family held the office for much of the following half century, and historians credit the first two Koprulu viziers with a temporary revival of Ottoman power.
442.explanation: Entrusting the state to an able minister both ended an immediate crisis and laid foundations that protected the empire for decades.
442.tie_back: The kural urges a ruler to cherish those who can remove troubles that have come and guard against those still to come, and Koprulu did both for the Ottoman throne.
442._accuracy_note: Shows an adviser who cured a present crisis and strengthened the state against future ones, but his methods were harsh and the sultan's role was largely passive.

443.event_title: Emperor Rudolf II welcomes Tycho Brahe to Prague
443.place: Prague and Benatky nad Jizerou, Bohemia (now Czech Republic)
443.event: After the great Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe left Denmark, the Holy Roman Emperor Rudolf II made him imperial mathematician in 1599, gave him a generous salary and provided the castle of Benatky near Prague for his observatory. In 1600 Tycho invited the young Johannes Kepler to work with him there. When Tycho died in 1601, Rudolf appointed Kepler to succeed him, and Kepler's planetary tables were later named the Rudolphine Tables in the emperor's honour.
443.explanation: By honouring and providing for great scholars, Rudolf made his court a centre of the astronomy that transformed European science.
443.tie_back: The kural calls it the rarest of all things to honour great people and make them one's own, and Rudolf drew two of the greatest astronomers of the age into his household.
443._accuracy_note: A good picture of honouring the great and binding them to oneself, though the relationship was patronage more than the close kinship the kural describes.

444.event_title: Lincoln appoints his rivals to his cabinet
444.place: Springfield, Illinois, and Washington, D.C., United States
444.event: After winning the presidency in 1860, Abraham Lincoln filled the most important posts in his cabinet with the men who had competed against him for the Republican nomination. William H. Seward, the front-runner he had defeated, became Secretary of State; Salmon P. Chase became Secretary of the Treasury; Edward Bates became Attorney General; and Simon Cameron became Secretary of War.
444.explanation: Lincoln chose to surround himself with powerful and experienced figures rather than loyal followers, gaining their abilities for the Union during the Civil War.
444.tie_back: The kural calls it the foremost strength to conduct oneself so that those greater than oneself become one's own, and Lincoln made his strongest rivals his closest colleagues.
444._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural, although Lincoln's colleagues were his equals or rivals in standing more than clearly greater than him.

445.event_title: Elizabeth I chooses William Cecil as her chief minister
445.event: On her accession to the English throne in November 1558, Elizabeth I appointed William Cecil, an experienced administrator, as her principal secretary of state. Cecil served her for about 40 years until his death in 1598, first as secretary and from 1572 as Lord Treasurer, having been made Baron Burghley in 1571. He handled almost all of the queen's formal correspondence and was her most trusted adviser through most of her reign.
445.explanation: Elizabeth's first and most lasting decision as queen was the choice of the minister through whose reports and judgement she would see her kingdom.
445.tie_back: The kural says a king must treat his counsellors as his eyes and therefore choose them with great care, and Elizabeth's careful choice of Cecil served her for four decades.
445._accuracy_note: A close match for choosing counsellors as one's eyes; the sources differ slightly on the exact day the appointment took effect.

446.event_title: Frederick the Wise shelters Martin Luther at the Wartburg
446.event: After the Diet of Worms in 1521, Emperor Charles V declared Martin Luther an outlaw. Luther's protector, Frederick III, Elector of Saxony, known as Frederick the Wise, arranged for him to be taken on the road and hidden at the Wartburg castle, where he lived in disguise for nearly a year. There Luther translated the New Testament into German, and it was published in 1522.
446.explanation: Under the protection of a respected prince and his circle, a man condemned by the most powerful ruler in Europe was able to continue his work unharmed.
446.tie_back: The kural says enemies can do nothing to one who lives within the company of the worthy, and Luther's protectors made the emperor's sentence powerless against him.
446._accuracy_note: Shows protection by worthy allies, but it rests on one powerful patron rather than on Luther's own membership of a fellowship of the virtuous.

447.event_title: Gandhi answers Tagore's public criticism with respect
447.event: In 1921 Rabindranath Tagore published an essay, The Call of Truth, in the Modern Review, criticising parts of Mahatma Gandhi's non-cooperation movement as a negative and inward-looking turning away from cooperation with the wider world. Gandhi replied in his journal Young India on 13 October 1921 in an essay he titled The Great Sentinel, engaging Tagore's arguments seriously. The two continued to debate openly in print over the following years while remaining close friends.
447.explanation: Gandhi kept the country's most respected critic close and answered him in public rather than dismissing him, and their exchange remains a model of principled disagreement.
447.tie_back: The kural asks who can ruin one who keeps companions able to rebuke him, and Gandhi honoured Tagore precisely as the friend who would tell him where he was wrong.
447._accuracy_note: A strong example of valuing a rebuking friend; Gandhi did not always accept Tagore's criticism, so the protective effect the kural promises is implied rather than shown.

448.event_title: Nicholas II takes personal command against his ministers' advice
448.event: In the late summer of 1915, with Russian armies in retreat, Tsar Nicholas II dismissed the commander in chief, Grand Duke Nicholas, and took supreme command himself, despite objections from his Council of Ministers. With the tsar away at headquarters, power in the capital passed largely to Empress Alexandra, and capable ministers were replaced by weaker figures, many favoured by Grigori Rasputin. The government lost the confidence of the country, and in March 1917 Nicholas was forced to abdicate.
448.explanation: By overruling and removing those who warned him, Nicholas cut himself off from correction at the moment his throne most needed it.
448.tie_back: The kural says an unguarded king with no one to rebuke him perishes even without enemies to destroy him, and Nicholas's monarchy collapsed from within.
448._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of a ruler silencing his critics and falling from within, though the pressures of the war also played a large part.

449.event_title: Emperor Maximilian of Mexico loses his French support
449.event: Archduke Maximilian of Austria became emperor of Mexico in 1864, his rule upheld by French troops sent by Napoleon III. Under pressure from the United States, Napoleon agreed in 1866 to withdraw, and the last French forces left in early 1867. Left with only a small army, Maximilian was besieged and captured at Queretaro by the republican forces of Benito Juarez and was executed in June 1867.
449.explanation: Maximilian's empire had no foundation of its own, and once the outside support that propped it up was removed, it fell within months.
449.tie_back: The kural says there is no stability for those without strong support to prop them up, just as there is no profit without capital, and Maximilian's throne collapsed when its prop was withdrawn.
449._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it vividly shows a ruler falling without support, but the kural speaks of the support of the worthy, and the French intervention was not that.

450.event_title: Louis XVI dismisses the reforming minister Turgot
450.event: Anne-Robert-Jacques Turgot, appointed controller general of finances by Louis XVI in 1774, proposed the Six Edicts, which among other things abolished compulsory road labour by peasants and the Paris guilds. The privileged orders, court factions and the Parlement of Paris opposed the reforms strongly. In May 1776 Louis XVI gave way and dismissed Turgot, and most of his reforms were abandoned.
450.explanation: By giving up an able and honest minister to quiet powerful opponents, Louis XVI lost one of the best chances of reforming France's finances before the crisis that led to the Revolution.
450.tie_back: The kural warns that abandoning the friendship of the good is ten times worse than the hostility of many, and Louis chose to placate many opponents at the cost of his best counsel.
450._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of giving up good counsel to avoid opposition; the claim that Turgot's reforms could have prevented the Revolution is a historians' debate, not a fact.
